title: Gut microbiome-derived bacterial extracellular vesicles in patients with solid tumours
projectDescription: In this study, we performed a comparative analysis of gut microbiota composition and gut microbiome-derived bacterial extracellular vesicles (bEVs) isolated from patients with solid tumours and healthy controls. After isolating bEVs from the faeces of solid tumour patients and healthy controls, we performed spectrometry analysis of their proteomes and next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the 16S gene. We also investigated the gut microbiomes of faeces from patientsand controls using 16S rRNA sequencing. Machine learning was used to classify the samples into patients and controls based on their bEVs and faecal microbiomes.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Proteins were extracted from extracellular vesicles(EVs) using Friedman’s methanol precipitation method with some modifications. 20 μL of isolated protein sample was loaded onto commercial 12 % separating gels (Mini-Protean TGX, Bio-Rad), electrophoresis was run at 110 V for 10–15 min followed by fixing of the gel in 50 % ethanol and 10 % acetic acid for 30 min in a shaker at room temperature. The fixed gel was stained with 20 ml of 1x Sypro Ruby protein stain at room temperature overnight and then destained with 5 % acetic acid for 5 min in a shaker. Protein bands were then visualised under UV light, cut, and stored in Eppendorf tubes. The gel pieces were dehydrated using 99 % ethanol and sent for mass spectrometry analysis. Isolated EV proteins were analysed by LC-ESI-MS/MS on a nanoflow HPLC system (Easy-nLC1200, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) attached to a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a nanoelectrospray ionisation source. Peptides were loaded on a trapping column and then separated on a 15-cm C18 column (75 μm x 15 cm, ReproSil-Pur 3 μm 120 Å C18-AQ; Dr. Maisch HPLC GmbH, Ammerbuch-Entringen, Germany). The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (water with 0·1% formic acid) and solvent B (acetonitrile/water (80:20 v/v) with 0·1 % formic acid). A linear 20-min gradient from 8 % to 43 % of solvent B was used to elute the peptides. Thermo Xcalibur 4.1 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to collect the MS data. An information-based acquisition method consisting of an Orbitrap MS survey scan with a mass range of 300–2,000 m/z was followed by HCD fragmentation for the 10 peptide ions with the highest intensity.
dataProcessingProtocol: Proteomics on MS data was performed using Peaks Studio software (version 10.6)28. Proteins were identified by searches in the UniProt Swissprot and UniProt trEMBL (UniProt release 2022_05) databases with a parent mass error tolerance of 10·0 ppm and fragment mass error tolerance set of 0·02 Da. A false discovery rate (FDR) of 1·0 % was fixed for both the peptide and protein identification. Proteins with at least one unique peptide and total protein coverage of supporting peptides 1 %, were considered identified. Only the top proteins with most assigned hits from each protein group were selected and reported. Negative controls were also analysed, and protein identifications made from the negative controls were excluded from the sample data. Taxonomic names were reported as they appeared in UniProt release 2023_03. Figures were drawn using Rstudio (2023.03.1 +446 for Windows) and R 4.3.0 using the ggplot2 package (version 3.4.2).
keywords: Bacterial extracellular vesicles; gut microbiome; solid tumour; proteomics
